slides.title: Protection vs Security
slides.body: Protection vs Security
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Protection vs Security

slides.title: Two Related Scopes
slides.body:
Two Related Scopes
Protection And Security
Protection is the mechanism controlling which process or user may access which resource
Security is the wider goal of defending the whole system against threats, internal and external
slides.notes:
Protection and security are related, but they are not the same.
Protection controls who can access what in the system. For example, whether a user is allowed to open a particular file.
Security is broader & protects the entire system from threats, like unauthorized access, malware, or attacks.
So, simply: Protection controls access, while security protects the overall system.

slides.title: Physical threats
slides.body:
Physical threats
Network threats
Human threats
OS-level protection
Two Related Scopes
Protection And Security
slides.notes: Security threats can come from different sources, so the system needs protection at multiple levels.1 Physical threats include theft, fire, or disasters that can damage hardware or cause data loss.2 Network threats include intrusion, packet sniffing, and unauthorized remote access.3 Human threats include social engineering and misuse by authorized users.4 OS-level protection ensures that users and processes can access only the resources they are permitted to use.

slides.title: Separating Policy Mechanism
slides.body:
Separating Policy Mechanism
Protection Mechanism
Protection supplies the enforcement machinery for access rules
policy is the separate decision of what those rules should be
slides.notes:
Here, we separate policy from mechanism.
Policy decides what should be allowed — for example, an administrator may decide that only certain users can access a file.
Mechanism is how the OS enforces that decision through kernel-enforced checks. These mechanisms are fixed and reusable for different policies.
So, policy is the decision, while mechanism is the enforcement.

slides.title: Separating Policy Mechanism
slides.body:
Separating Policy Mechanism
Protection Mechanism
Same mechanism serves many different policies
Policy can change without redesigning enforcement code
slides.notes:
The same mechanism can be used for different policies.
For example, the OS permission-checking mechanism can enforce different access rules.
So, if the policy changes, we don't need to redesign the enforcement mechanism.
Simply: the mechanism stays the same, while the policy can change.

slides.title: Analogy
slides.body:
Analogy
Protection Mechanism
slides.notes:
Think of traffic signals at a busy intersection. The signal system is the mechanism because it controls when vehicles can move. The timing rules set by traffic authorities are the policy.
Similarly, an OS protection mechanism enforces whatever access rules are defined by the policy.

slides.title: Why Protection Exists?
slides.body:
Why Protection Exists?
Goals Of Protection
Protection exists to keep shared systems reliable, not only to lock things down – misuse can be malicious or purely accidental
slides.notes: Protection makes sure that every process can access only the resources it is authorised to use. For example, one process should not be able to read or modify another process’s private memory.Protection also helps prevent damage caused by accidental mistakes, not just malicious actions. By giving a process limited permissions, a bug in that process is less likely to affect other parts of the system.This follows the least privilege principle: a process should receive only the permissions it needs to perform its task.Protection can also help identify problems when different system components interact incorrectly. Overall, protection helps keep the system isolated, reliable, and safer when something goes wrong.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
Goals
Security Defined
Security is the discipline of defending a system against threats, using protection as one tool alongside authentication, encryption and monitoring
slides.notes:
Security is about protecting the whole system from threats. Although ,Protection controls access, while security combines that with things like authentication, encryption, and monitoring to defend the system
A simple way to understand security is through these four goals.1 Prevent unauthorised disclosure of data
2 Prevent unauthorised modification of data
3 Keep legitimate access working under attack
4 Trace actions back to a responsible entity

slides.title: Relationship Summarised
slides.body:
Relationship Summarised
Protection Vs Security
Protection is one pillar inside the larger security effort; sound protection is necessary for security but never sufficient on its own
slides.notes: Refer to reading material

slides.title: Access Control
slides.body: Access Control
slides.notes: Now we will be learning about the Access Control

slides.title: Subjects Objects Operations
slides.body:
Subjects Objects Operations
Access Control Basics
Every protection policy reduces to three elements: who is asking, what they want to do, and on which resource
slides.notes:
Access control can be understood using three simple questions: who is asking, what do they want to do,The OS uses these three elements to decide whether the requested action should be allowed or denied. and what resource are they trying to access?1 Process or user requesting access
2 Resource being protected – file, device, memory segment
3 Action requested – read, write, execute, switch
4 Formal model recording every allowed combination

slides.title: Rows Columns Rights
slides.body:
Rows Columns Rights
Access Matrix Model
1. Rows
2. Columns
3. Cells
The access matrix places every domain against every object, with each cell holding the operations that domain may perform on that object
slides.notes:
An access matrix is simply a table that shows who can do what to which resource.
The rows represent the subjects or domains, such as different users or processes.
The columns represent the objects, such as files or devices
Finally, each cell contains the allowed operations, like read, write, or execute.
So, to check permission, we find the subject’s row and the object’s column, and then look at the rights in that cell.

slides.title: Rows Columns Rights
slides.body:
Rows Columns Rights
Access Matrix Model
4. Switch
5. Matrix
slides.notes:
A switch means that the system can change from one protection domain to another. For example, a process may switch from one domain to another when it needs a different set of permissions.
The matrix is the complete table that records all the permissions between domains and objects.So, the main idea is: the matrix records the rights, while the switch allows movement between protection domains when permitted.

slides.title: Analogy
slides.body:
Analogy
Access Matrix Model
slides.notes: Think of a hotel keycard system. A guest is like a subject, and a room is like an object. The keycard defines which rooms the guest can access. Similarly, an OS access matrix defines which operations a subject can perform on each object.

slides.title: Three Domains Example
slides.body:
Three Domains Example
Worked Matrix Trace
A three-process matrix over two files and a printer shows how a real protection state is recorded in the model discussed above
slides.notes:
Here we have a simple example of an access matrix with three domains or processes.
The matrix records which process can access which resource, such as two files and a printer.
For example, one process might have read and write permission on File 1, while another process may only have read permission.
The printer can also have its own permission, such as print.

slides.title: Three Domains Example
slides.body:
Three Domains Example
Worked Matrix Trace
Has zero rights on /etc/shadow – explicit denial by absence
Empty cell means no implicit access, unlike file-permission defaults
Can switch into PID 5820 – controlled privilege narrowing
slides.notes:
Let’s trace this matrix with three different processes.
PID 4312 is the owner, so it has read and write access to both files. It can also switch to PID 5820, which means it can move into that controlled privilege domain.
PID 5820 has more limited permissions. It can read /etc/shadow, but it cannot access the reports document. It can also print using the printer.
PID 6603 is the guest. It can only read the reports document and has no access to the other resources.
Notice that an empty cell means no access. The process does not automatically get permission just because the resource exists.
So this matrix gives us a precise picture of what each process is allowed to do with each resource.

slides.title: Four Storage Techniques
slides.body:
Four Storage Techniques
Matrix Implementation
Storing the full sparse matrix wastes space, so operating systems keep only the non-empty cells using one of four techniques
slides.notes:
An access matrix can become very large, and most of its cells are usually empty. So storing the entire matrix would waste space.
Instead, operating systems use different ways to store only the permissions that actually exist.
A global table stores entries as domain, object, and rights.It is simple, but searching through many entries can be slow.
An ACL, or Access Control List, stores the permissions with the object itself.
In other words, we look at a file and ask, ‘Who is allowed to access this file, and what can they do?

slides.title: Four Storage Techniques
slides.body:
Four Storage Techniques
Matrix Implementation
Storing the full sparse matrix wastes space, so operating systems keep only the non-empty cells using one of four techniques
slides.notes:
Two more ways to implement the access matrix are capability lists and lock-key mechanisms.
With a capability list, we store the permissions with the domain. So we ask: ‘What resources can this process access, and what can it do with them?’
For example, a process might have: File A — read/write, File B — read, Printer — print.
With lock-key, the object has a lock and the domain has a matching key. Access is allowed only when the key matches the lock.
So remember the difference: ACL focuses on the object — who can access me? Capability list focuses on the domain — what can I access?

slides.title: Trade-offs Compared
slides.body:
Trade-offs Compared
ACL Vs Capability
Access-control lists and capability lists slice the same matrix differently, trading revocation ease against transfer flexibility
slides.notes:
Here we are comparing ACL and capability lists. Both represent the same permissions, but they look at them from different sides.
With an ACL, permissions are stored with the object. So we ask: ‘Who can access this file?’ It is also easier to revoke access because we simply remove the user from the file’s list.
With a capability list, permissions are stored with the domain. So we ask: ‘What can this process access?’ Capabilities are easier to pass or delegate to another process.
So the main trade-off is: ACLs make revoking access easier, while capability lists make transferring access easier

slides.title: Categories And Traits
slides.body:
Categories And Traits
Malware Overview
Malware is software deliberately designed to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a system. Categories differ mainly in host-dependency and self-replication
slides.notes:
Malware means software that is intentionally created to harm a system or gain access without permission.
There are different types of malware, and an important difference is whether it needs another program to spread or can spread by itself.
A virus attaches itself to a legitimate file or program and spreads when that infected file is executed.
A worm does not need to attach to another program. It can replicate and spread on its own, often through a network.
A Trojan looks like legitimate or useful software, but once the user runs it, it performs malicious actions.
So, the easy way to remember them is: virus attaches, worm spreads by itself, Trojan disguises itself.

slides.title: Categories And Traits
slides.body:
Categories And Traits
Malware Overview
Malware is software deliberately designed to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a system. Categories differ mainly in host-dependency and self-replication
slides.notes:
Now let’s look at three more types of malware.
Ransomware blocks access to files or systems, usually by encrypting the data, and demands payment to restore access.
Spyware secretly monitors the user or system and collects information, such as browsing activity or sensitive data.
A rootkit is designed to hide malicious activity and maintain unauthorised access to the system. It can operate at a very low level, making it difficult to detect.

slides.title: Host-Dependent Infection
slides.body:
Host-Dependent Infection
Virus Mechanism
Dormant phase
Propagation
Triggering
Payload
1
2
3
4
A virus is code that attaches itself to a legitimate executable or document and activates only when that host file runs
slides.notes:
Here we can see how a virus infects a host file.
First is the dormant phase—the virus is attached to a legitimate file but is not active yet.
Next is propagation. When the infected file is shared or copied, the virus can spread to other files or systems.
Then comes triggering. A particular condition, such as opening theinfected file or reaching a specific date, causes the virus to activate.
Finally, the payload is the actual malicious action—for example, damaging files or disrupting the system.
So the simple flow is: stay hidden → spread → get triggered → perform the malicious action.

slides.title: Analogy
slides.body:
Analogy
Virus Mechanism
slides.notes: Think of a seed attached to a plant. The seed stays with the plant until it is carried to another place, where it can grow and spread. Similarly, a computer virus attaches to a host file and spreads when that file is executed

slides.title: Self-Replicating Spread
slides.body:
Self-Replicating Spread
A worm is a standalone program that replicates itself and spreads across networks without attaching to a host file or needing user execution
Worm Propagation
slides.notes:
Unlike a virus, a worm is a standalone program, so it does not need to attach itself to another file.
A worm can find vulnerable systems through a network and spread automatically, without waiting for the user to open a file.
Because it can replicate quickly, it may consume a lot of network bandwidth and system resources.
Once it reaches a system, it can also carry a payload, such as installing a backdoor or ransomware.
So the main difference to remember is: a virus needs a host file, but a worm can spread independently.

slides.title: Analogy
slides.body:
Analogy
Worm Propagation
slides.notes: A wildfire jumps from tree to tree on its own once it starts, needing no one to carry the flame — just as a worm spreads across a network without any user action.

slides.title: Disguised Malicious Code
slides.body:
Disguised Malicious Code
Trojan Payloads
A trojan is malware disguised as legitimate or useful software, relying on the user to install it voluntarily; it does not self-replicate
Remote Access Trojan (RAT)
Backdoor trojan
Keylogger trojan
Dropper trojan
slides.notes: A Trojan is malware that pretends to be legitimate or useful software. It usually depends on the user installing or running it, and unlike a worm, it does not self-replicate.Different Trojan types perform different malicious actions. A Remote Access Trojan (RAT) provides unauthorised remote access to the system. A Backdoor Trojan secretly provides unauthorised access to the system. A Keylogger Trojan records keystrokes and can capture sensitive information. A Dropper Trojan installs or delivers other malware onto the system.So remember: a Trojan disguises itself, the user runs it, and then it performs its malicious action.

slides.title: Threats Compared
slides.body:
Threats Compared
Virus Worm Trojan
The three classic malware types differ chiefly in host-dependency, replication ability and how they gain entry into a system
slides.notes:
Let’s compare these three malware types based on the key traits shown here.
A virus needs a host file and self-replicates through infected files. It usually requires the user to run that infected file.
A worm does not need a host file. It self-replicates automatically, spreading through network vulnerabilities without user action.
A Trojan does not need a host file because the malware itself is disguised as legitimate software. It does not self-replicate and usually depends on the user installing it through social engineering.
So the key difference is: virus spreads through infected files, worm spreads through network vulnerabilities, and Trojan gets in by disguising itself

slides.title: Ransomware, spyware and rootkits combine the classic triad's mechanisms with a s
slides.body:
Ransomware, spyware and rootkits combine the classic triad's mechanisms with a specific payload goal, and real incidents show the scale of resulting damage
Impact And Examples
Malware In Practice
slides.notes:
Here we can see how these types of malware appear in real attacks.
Ransomware may arrive through a Trojan and then spread through the network like a worm.
Spyware is often hidden inside a Trojan installer and is used to secretly collect information.
Rootkits work at a deeper level by modifying kernel structures so the malware can hide from detection.
Some well-known examples include the Morris worm from 1988 and the Zeus banking Trojan from 2007.
So, different malware types can also combine their techniques to make an attack more effective.

slides.title: Vulnerabilities
slides.body: Vulnerabilities
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Vulnerabilities.

slides.title: Two Exploit Classes
slides.body:
Two Exploit Classes
Vulnerabilities Landscape
A vulnerability is a weakness a threat exploits to break through the protection boundaries a system defines
slides.notes:
A vulnerability is a weakness that an attacker can use to break through the system’s protection.
There are four examples shown here.
A buffer overflow happens when more data is put into a memory buffer than it can hold.
Privilege escalation means an attacker gains permissions higher than they should have.
Vertical escalation is moving from a lower-privileged user to a higher-privileged user, such as an administrator.
Horizontal escalation means accessing another user’s resources while staying at roughly the same privilege level.

slides.title: Buffer overflow happens when a program writes more data into a fixed-size buffer
slides.body:
Buffer overflow happens when a program writes more data into a fixed-size buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory
Stack Overwrite Flaw
Buffer Overflow
slides.notes:
Buffer overflow happens when a program puts more data into a fixed-size memory area than it can hold.
A common cause is unchecked input, where the program does not properly check how much data it receives.
On the stack, extra data can overwrite nearby information, including the saved return address.
If that return address is changed, the program may jump to an unintended location. The result can be anything from a simple crash to unauthorised code execution.
So the key idea is: too much input → memory gets overwritten → program behaviour can be changed

slides.title: Analogy
slides.body:
Analogy
Buffer Overflow
slides.notes: Imagine a glass filled to the top. If you keep pouring, the extra water spills into the nearby area and may disturb other things.Similarly, when a program writes more data than a buffer can hold, the extra data can overwrite nearby memory, including important information such as the return address, potentially causing the program to crash or behave unexpectedly.

slides.title: Overwriting Return Address
slides.body:
Overwriting Return Address
Stack Smashing Trace
A concrete stack layout shows how an oversized input overwrites the saved return address with an attacker-chosen value 
Control transfers to 0x7ffee050 on function return, executing the attacker's injected code instead of the caller
slides.notes:
Here we can see what happens when a buffer overflow overwrites the saved return address.
Normally, when a function finishes, the return address tells the program where to go back.
If oversized input overwrites that address with an attacker-chosen value, the program can be redirected somewhere else.
In this example, the return address is changed to 0x7ffee050, so when the function returns, control goes to that location instead of returning normally.
The key idea is: overwrite the return address → change where the program continues execution

slides.title: Overwriting Return Address
slides.body:
Overwriting Return Address
Stack Smashing Trace
slides.notes:
Let’s look at the stack before and after the overflow.
Before the overflow, the buffer at 0x7ffee010 contains the input, the saved frame pointer is at 0x7ffee020, and the return address at 0x7ffee028 tells the program where to return.
After the overflow, the extra input fills the buffer and overwrites the nearby values. Most importantly, the return address changes from 0x00401234 to 0x7ffee050.
So when the function returns, the program uses this new address instead of the original one, changing where execution continues.
The important takeaway is: the overflow doesn't just affect the buffer—
it can overwrite important control information stored next to it.

slides.title: Privilege escalation exploits a flaw to obtain permissions beyond what was legit
slides.body:
Privilege escalation exploits a flaw to obtain permissions beyond what was legitimately granted, often the end goal of a buffer overflow exploit
Gaining Higher Rights
Privilege Escalation
slides.notes: Privilege escalation means gaining permissions that the user or process was not originally supposed to have.For example, an attacker may exploit a buffer overflow to make a compromised process run with the owner’s higher privileges.Another example is misusing a setuid or setgid program, which runs with the owner’s permissions.An attacker could also exploit an unpatched kernel or service vulnerability to gain higher privileges.Finally, in a horizontal escalation, the attacker stays at a similar privilege level but gains access to another user’s data, such as through stolen credentials.

slides.title: Analogy
slides.body:
Analogy
Privilege Escalation
slides.notes: Imagine an employee has a keycard that allows access only to the ground floor. If a flaw lets that keycard open the executive suite, the employee has gained access they were never authorised to have.Similarly, privilege escalation happens when an attacker exploits a weakness to gain permissions beyond their original access.

slides.title: Defense Techniques Compared
slides.body:
Defense Techniques Compared
Mitigating Both Flaws
Buffer overflow and privilege escalation are stopped by different layers of defence, from compiler-level checks to strict privilege design
slides.notes:
Here we are comparing the defenses for the two vulnerabilities.
For buffer overflow, defenses include stack canaries, ASLR, DEP/NX, and bounds-checked functions. These mainly protect memory and prevent unintended code execution.
For privilege escalation, we use least privilege, timely patching, sandboxing, and audit logging. These reduce the permissions an attacker can gain and help detect or contain misuse.
So the key point is that different layers provide different defenses—from checks in how software handles memory to careful design of user and process privileges
tables: Stack canaries, ASLR, DEP/NX bit, bounds-checked functions
Least-privilege principle, timely patching, sandboxing, audit logging

slides.title: Defenses
slides.body: Defenses
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Defenses

slides.title: Malware, overflow and privilege escalation are countered by three complementary
slides.body:
Malware, overflow and privilege escalation are countered by three complementary defense layers, not one silver bullet
Auth Encryption Practices
Defense Layers
slides.notes:
Here we use three layers of defense. Authentication checks who the user is, encryption protects the data, and security best practices reduce possible attack points. The key idea is that these layers work together rather than relying on just one defense
Here point to note is : Here, the main point is that malware, buffer overflows, and privilege escalation need multiple defenses. Authentication, encryption, and good security practices each protect a different layer. So there is no single security measure that can stop every type of attack.

slides.title: Passwords Biometrics MFA
slides.body:
Passwords Biometrics MFA
Authentication Factors
Authentication proves a claimed identity using one or more independent factors before access is granted
slides.notes:
Authentication is about proving a claimed identity before access is granted. It can use one or more independent factors.
The three factors shown here are: knowledge, such as a password; possession, such as having a phone or security device; and inherence, meaning something you are, such as a fingerprint.

slides.title: Authentication proves a claimed identity using one or more independent factors b
slides.body:
Authentication proves a claimed identity using one or more independent factors before access is granted
Passwords Biometrics MFA
Authentication Factors
Weakness
MFA
slides.notes: Authentication can have weaknesses if we depend on only one factor, such as a password. If that factor is compromised, the attacker may gain access. MFA reduces this weakness by combining multiple independent factors, so compromising one factor alone is not enough to get access

slides.title: Analogy
slides.body:
Analogy
Authentication Factors
slides.notes: A bank locker needs the customer's key AND the banker's key together, from two different people —> exactly as multi-factor authentication needs two different factor categories together, not two of the same kind.

slides.title: Encryption transforms readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using a key,
slides.body:
Encryption transforms readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using a key, protecting data at rest and in transit
Symmetric Vs Asymmetric
Encryption Fundamentals
slides.notes: Encryption protects data by converting readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using a key.With symmetric encryption, the same shared key is used to encrypt and decrypt the data, such as AES. The challenge is securely sharing that key.With asymmetric encryption, a public key is used for encryption, while the private key is used for decryption. It can also support digital signatures, which help verify who sent the data and confirm that it was not modified.So, the main difference is how the keys are used and managed.

slides.title: Symmetric
slides.body:
Symmetric
Asymmetric
Analogy
Encryption Fundamentals
slides.notes: Sharing one house key with a trusted neighbour is symmetric encryption; dropping a letter into a public mailbox that only the owner's private key can open is asymmetric — just as one shared key locks and unlocks in symmetric encryption, while a public key locks and a distinct private key unlocks in asymmetric encryption.

slides.title: Algorithms And Use Cases
slides.body:
Algorithms And Use Cases
Symmetric Vs Asymmetric
Speed and key-management needs decide which approach applies where; most real systems use both together
slides.notes:
Here we compare the two approaches. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key, so it is faster and has low overhead. AES is a common example, and it is mainly used for bulk data encryption.
Asymmetric encryption uses a public and private key pair. It is slower and more compute-heavy, but the public key can be shared openly. RSA and ECC are common examples, and it is useful for key exchange and digital signatures.
In practice, systems often use both together—asymmetric encryption for securely establishing keys, and symmetric encryption for the actual data.

slides.title: Defense In Depth
slides.body:
Defense In Depth
Security Best Practices
No single mechanism stops every threat, so systems layer independent controls so one failure does not expose everything
slides.notes:
Defense in depth means we do not depend on one security mechanism. We use multiple independent controls, so if one fails, the others still provide protection.
Regular patching fixes known vulnerabilities, including buffer-overflow and privilege-escalation bugs. We also encrypt data both at rest and in transit, while keeping encryption keys separate from the data.
Finally, strong authentication and MFA should be used especially for privileged accounts, because compromising these accounts can give an attacker much greater access

slides.title: Defense In Depth
slides.body:
Defense In Depth
Security Best Practices
No single mechanism stops every threat, so systems layer independent controls so one failure does not expose everything
slides.notes: Logging and monitoring are important because prevention is not always enough. If someone tries to access something they should not, logs can help detect that activity and identify policy violations.We should also disable services we do not use. This reduces the attack surface by removing unnecessary services that could be targeted by attackers.

slides.title: OS Security & Protection
slides.body:
Protection vs Security

slides.notes:
And that brings us to the end of our Operating Systems journey. Look how far you've come — from what a process is, through scheduling, synchronization, and memory, all the way to file systems, storage, and I/O Every one of those pieces is working together right now on the device in front of you.
More than the topics, I hope you're leaving with a way of thinking — asking who gets a resource, when, and how to keep it fair, fast, and safe.
Keep the curiosity alive.
Thank you for your energy and attention throughout the course;
All the best, keep learning and Keep growing
